required_facts.statement: A GuardDuty finding contains a finding type, severity, affected resource and details of suspicious activity.
Inspect resource identity, activity timestamps and finding details, and preserve the evidence supporting investigation.
Follow the established investigation and escalation procedure for the finding type rather than taking destructive action from severity alone.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A GuardDuty finding has a severity label, but an operator needs its resource and activity evidence before responding. Use the established investigation path rather than acting destructively from severity alone.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A GuardDuty finding contains a finding type, severity, affected resource and details of suspicious activity.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect resource identity, activity timestamps and finding details, and preserve the evidence supporting investigation.

Follow the established investigation and escalation procedure for the finding type rather than taking destructive action from severity alone.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Open the supplied finding and record its type, severity, affected resource identity and activity timestamps. Inspect the detailed suspicious activity and preserve the supporting evidence. Route the investigation through the established procedure for that finding type. If the finding is severe, include that urgency in the response context, but do not turn it into an unsupported conclusion that the resource is compromised or permission to destroy it. The example teaches bounded finding triage: identify what the finding says, retain the evidence and follow the approved escalation procedure.

A finding timeline should retain the activity timestamps supplied in the finding rather than substituting the time someone opened it. Resource identity narrows which workload the suspicious activity concerns, while type and detail inform the established investigation path. If those details are incomplete, preserve the available evidence and escalate under the procedure. Missing detail is not a basis for asserting an attack mechanism or destroying the resource.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A severity label alone is not the complete investigation or an instruction to take destructive action. Inspect resource identity, timestamps and activity details, preserve the evidence and follow the established finding-type procedure.

video_need.reason: A short finding walkthrough helps locate resource, timestamp and activity evidence while text fully bounds the response decision.

practice_anchor.objective: Triage one supplied GuardDuty finding using a read-only finding interface and its established investigation and escalation procedure. Record the finding type, severity, affected resource identity, activity timestamps and suspicious activity details; preserve the supporting evidence and identify the procedure-supported next step.
practice_anchor.success: The triage record accurately identifies the affected identity or resource, retains the supplied activity timestamps and supporting finding details, and selects the next investigation or escalation step specified by the supplied procedure. It neither asserts compromise without supporting evidence nor takes destructive action from severity alone.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the finding type, severity, affected resource identity, activity timestamps and suspicious activity details visible in a representative GuardDuty finding, distinguishing activity timestamps from the time the finding was opened.

teaching_notes: Do not invent compromise conclusions or specialist incident-containment actions.

required_facts.statement: S3 bucket policies can grant or deny object operations to specified principals and resource paths.
Give approved audit writers and readers only their required actions on the intended bucket or object ARNs; inspect other applicable grants and denies.
Test a write and read with approved identities and a read with the unapproved identity; encryption or retention settings do not replace authorization checks.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Audit objects need approved write and read access without unintended readers. Inspect authorization as its own control, not as an effect of encryption or retention.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: S3 bucket policies can grant or deny object operations to specified principals and resource paths.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Give approved audit writers and readers only their required actions on the intended bucket or object ARNs; inspect other applicable grants and denies.

Test a write and read with approved identities and a read with the unapproved identity; encryption or retention settings do not replace authorization checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Scope the supplied bucket policy to the approved writers/readers, required actions and intended bucket or object ARNs. Inspect other applicable grants and denies. Test an approved write, an approved read and an unapproved read, recording the identity and resource path for each. Those results verify the requested access boundary; encryption and retention settings do not replace these tests.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Protected storage settings are not authorization evidence. Even with encryption or retention configured, inspect applicable grants/denies and test approved and unapproved object operations.

video_need.reason: A short approved/unapproved policy-test comparison helps locate audit-object authorization evidence independently of storage controls.

practice_anchor.objective: Apply least-privilege access to the supplied S3 audit bucket policy using the supplied approved writers, approved readers and audit paths. Inspect other applicable grants and denies, then test an approved write, an approved read and an unapproved read.
practice_anchor.success: The policy grants approved writers and readers only their required actions on the intended bucket or object ARNs without broadening principal access. Applicable grants and denies have been inspected. The approved write and read succeed, and the unapproved read is denied, with the identity, resource path and result recorded for each test. Encryption or retention settings are not treated as authorization evidence.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the scoped bucket-policy statements alongside the three authorization test results, making each principal, requested action, resource ARN and allowed or denied outcome visible.

teaching_notes: Use supplied audit paths and policy; do not broaden principal access for convenience.

context.concept_name: Audit KMS-backed audit-storage encryption (SSE-KMS): verify encryption and KMS key-use authority; key-use authority is required for SSE-KMS, not SSE-S3

required_facts.statement: SSE-KMS encrypts S3 objects with an AWS KMS key, while SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys.
Reading an SSE-KMS object requires both s3:GetObject permission and kms:Decrypt authority for its key; SSE-S3 does not require KMS key-use permission.
Configure the supplied KMS key as bucket default encryption and test reads with approved object/key authority and with KMS use denied; inspect the object’s encryption metadata.

misconceptions.statement: Changing bucket default encryption does not re-encrypt objects that already exist; their individual encryption settings still matter.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An audit reader can address an S3 object but still lacks the required KMS authority. Separate object access, key authority and the individual object's encryption metadata before interpreting the read result.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: SSE-KMS encrypts S3 objects with an AWS KMS key, while SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Reading an SSE-KMS object requires both s3:GetObject permission and kms:Decrypt authority for its key; SSE-S3 does not require KMS key-use permission.

Configure the supplied KMS key as bucket default encryption and test reads with approved object/key authority and with KMS use denied; inspect the object’s encryption metadata.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Configure the supplied KMS key as the bucket's default encryption. For the supplied SSE-KMS object, test a read under approved s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt authority. Then run the case where KMS use is denied and inspect the result. Read the object's encryption metadata to confirm what applies to that object. Changing bucket default encryption does not re-encrypt existing objects, so a default setting alone is not proof of an older object's encryption. Compare this with the stated SSE-S3 boundary: S3-managed-key encryption does not require KMS key-use permission. Keep those two encryption models distinct in the evidence instead of adding a KMS requirement to every S3 read.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Bucket default encryption does not change the individual encryption of objects that already exist. Inspect object metadata. Also, SSE-KMS read access needs both object permission and KMS Decrypt authority; SSE-S3 does not require KMS key-use permission.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content: Changing bucket default encryption does not re-encrypt objects that already exist; their individual encryption settings still matter.

video_need.reason: Object permissions, KMS authority and individual encryption metadata form distinct boundaries best clarified with an access-path diagram.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure the supplied KMS key as default encryption on one sandbox audit bucket. Inspect the supplied SSE-KMS object's encryption metadata, then test reads using prepared identities with approved object/key authority and with KMS use denied. Compare the KMS authority requirement with SSE-S3.
practice_anchor.success: The bucket default identifies the supplied KMS key, and the object's metadata confirms SSE-KMS and its key. The read with approved s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt authority succeeds; the read with s3:GetObject allowed but KMS use denied fails. The learner identifies that SSE-S3 needs no KMS key-use authority and that changing the bucket default does not re-encrypt existing objects.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show an audit reader's SSE-KMS access path with separate s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt authorization boundaries, alongside an SSE-S3 path with no KMS key-use requirement. Distinguish bucket default encryption from the individual object's encryption metadata.

teaching_notes: Keep existing-object/default distinction explicit; do not invent key-policy setup or re-encryption procedures.

coverage.learning_objective: Authorize or block Terraform EC2 plan impact, with mandatory destruction review

required_facts.statement: A Terraform plan describes proposed additions, updates, deletions and replacements based on configuration, state and observed infrastructure.
Create a saved plan with terraform plan -out=PLAN_FILE and inspect it with terraform show PLAN_FILE; replacement includes destruction and creation, not merely an in-place update.

Compare affected resource identities and every proposed action, including the mandatory deletion case, with the supplied scope and impact criteria and record accept or block with plan evidence; review does not require destructive execution.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A proposed Terraform change can remove infrastructure even when its description sounds like an update. Inspect the saved plan's action types and resource identities before recording a scope-and-impact decision.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Terraform plan describes proposed additions, updates, deletions and replacements based on configuration, state and observed infrastructure.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Create a saved plan with terraform plan -out=PLAN_FILE and inspect it with terraform show PLAN_FILE; replacement includes destruction and creation, not merely an in-place update.

Compare affected resource identities and every proposed action, including the mandatory deletion case, with the supplied scope and impact criteria and record accept or block with plan evidence; review does not require destructive execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Create the saved plan with terraform plan -out=PLAN_FILE and inspect terraform show PLAN_FILE. In the supplied review case, compare each addition, update, deletion and replacement with the approved scope and impact criteria. A replacement includes destruction and creation, not just an in-place edit. Include the mandatory deletion case in the review and record accept or block with the relevant plan evidence. This task does not require destructive execution to demonstrate that a planned deletion was identified. Keep the affected resource identities beside the actions so the decision applies to the actual plan rather than a general opinion that Terraform changes are safe.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Replacement is not merely an in-place update, and review does not require executing a deletion. Inspect every proposed action, including the supplied deletion case, and record the accept/block decision from plan and impact evidence.

video_need.reason: Plan action markers and resource identities benefit from a read-only review demonstration, including deletion and replacement cases.

practice_anchor.objective: Provision one EC2 instance using the supplied preapproved Terraform configuration and apply scaffold. Create and inspect a subsequent saved EC2 change plan, compare every affected resource identity and proposed action against supplied scope and impact criteria, and record accept or block with supporting evidence. Include a mandatory deletion case without executing destructive changes.
practice_anchor.success: One EC2 instance is provisioned through the supplied preapproved scaffold. The review identifies additions, updates, replacements and deletions in the supplied cases, treats replacement as destruction plus creation, and records an evidence-backed accept/block decision against the supplied criteria. No destructive review plan is applied.

live_code.required_skill: Use the supplied EC2 provisioning scaffold, save and inspect a Terraform plan, and evaluate its resource-level scope and destructive impact.
allowed_syntax: Supplied preapproved Terraform HCL for one EC2 instance with a pinned provider
terraform apply PLAN_FILE only for the supplied preapproved initial provisioning plan
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a prepared sandbox, a preapproved single-EC2 configuration and initial apply scaffold, followed by supplied EC2 change cases and explicit scope and impact criteria. The cases collectively include addition, in-place update, replacement and mandatory deletion; subsequent plans are reviewed only.
live_code.observable_success: The initial scaffold provisions one EC2 instance. Saved-plan inspection produces a review record pairing each affected EC2 resource identity with its proposed action, relevant plan evidence, applicable approval criterion and accept/block decision. Replacement is recorded as destructive, the deletion case is explicitly evaluated, and no destructive changes are executed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the saved EC2 plan's resource identities and addition, update, replacement and deletion markers visible alongside annotations linking each action to the supplied scope and impact criteria and the recorded accept/block decision.

teaching_notes: Do not execute destructive review cases; keep replacement controls for their later concept.

coverage.learning_objective: Preview a fleet operation with a dry run

required_facts.statement: For EC2 API operations that support DryRun, the dry-run request checks permissions without executing the operation; DryRunOperation indicates sufficient permission and UnauthorizedOperation indicates insufficient permission.
Use the supplied fleet wrapper’s preview mode, inspect its proposed targets and actions and compare them with approved scope without enabling mutation.
Dry-run permission success does not guarantee later operation success or provide a universal preview of every AWS service’s changes.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Before a supplied fleet wrapper may mutate resources, its preview should be compared with the approved targets and actions. Keep wrapper preview separate from the more limited permission check offered by supported EC2 DryRun operations.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: For EC2 API operations that support DryRun, the dry-run request checks permissions without executing the operation; DryRunOperation indicates sufficient permission and UnauthorizedOperation indicates insufficient permission.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the supplied fleet wrapper’s preview mode, inspect its proposed targets and actions and compare them with approved scope without enabling mutation.

Dry-run permission success does not guarantee later operation success or provide a universal preview of every AWS service’s changes.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Run the supplied wrapper's preview mode without enabling mutation. Compare its proposed targets and actions with the approved fleet scope and record any discrepancy. For the supplied EC2 operation that supports DryRun, interpret DryRunOperation as sufficient permission and UnauthorizedOperation as insufficient permission; the dry-run request does not execute that operation. A permission-success result is not a guarantee that a later real operation will succeed. Nor is EC2 DryRun a universal preview of every AWS service's changes. The wrapper's proposed-action evidence and the EC2 permission result address different questions, so retain them separately when deciding whether the supplied task is ready for approval.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: DryRunOperation is permission success for a supported EC2 dry-run request, not proof that a real operation ran. Dry-run permission success also does not guarantee later success or provide a service-wide change preview.

video_need.reason: Wrapper previews and supported EC2 dry-run permission outcomes benefit from a side-by-side nonmutating demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Run one supplied fleet operation in the wrapper's preview mode and compare its proposed targets and actions with the supplied approved scope, without enabling mutation.
practice_anchor.success: Preview mode remains enabled and mutation remains disabled. The learner identifies whether the proposed targets and actions match the approved scope and records any discrepancies.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied wrapper's proposed targets and actions alongside the approved fleet scope, with preview mode and disabled mutation visibly indicated. Separately show supported EC2 DryRun outcomes as permission evidence, not execution results or guarantees of later success.

teaching_notes: Use supplied wrapper preview; do not generalize DryRun to unsupported operations or services.

required_facts.statement: A fleet command has separate invocation results for individual targets, which may differ within one command.
Inspect invocation statuses and outputs and record successful, failed and unresolved targets separately.
Use target-specific results to choose the scoped follow-up rather than blindly repeating the entire operation on already successful targets.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A fleet command may succeed on some targets and fail on others. Follow-up needs a target-by-target result map so that successful work is not blindly repeated.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A fleet command has separate invocation results for individual targets, which may differ within one command.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect invocation statuses and outputs and record successful, failed and unresolved targets separately.

Use target-specific results to choose the scoped follow-up rather than blindly repeating the entire operation on already successful targets.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
For an illustrative three-target command, inspect each invocation status and output. If node A succeeded, node B failed and node C is unresolved, record those three categories with their target identities. Choose the supplied scoped follow-up using those individual outcomes. Do not label the unresolved node failed without evidence, and do not repeat the entire operation merely because one target failed. The separate invocation results are the basis for follow-up; a single overall command label cannot replace them. Keep the successful targets visible so the next operator can avoid treating the entire fleet as untouched.

The follow-up record should retain what is known and what remains unresolved. For node A, successful output is evidence of completion; for node B, retain the failure evidence; for node C, keep the unresolved status until inspection establishes an outcome. This distinction prevents the next operator from treating uncertainty as permission to repeat a mutation on every target. Use only the supplied scoped follow-up.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Partial failure is not the same as total failure. Successful, failed and unresolved targets need separate records. Use those results for scoped follow-up rather than blindly repeating the operation on already successful targets.

video_need.reason: A per-target success/failure/unresolved result table makes partial fleet outcomes and scoped follow-up substantially clearer.

practice_anchor.objective: Inspect supplied invocation statuses and outputs for one operation on node A, node B and node C. Record each target as successful, failed or unresolved, then select the supplied target-specific follow-up appropriate to each outcome.
practice_anchor.success: Node A's successful result remains recorded and is excluded from repeat execution. Node B is reported as failed with its failure evidence and the supplied scoped follow-up. Node C remains separately recorded as unresolved pending further inspection. No fleet-wide rerun or invented remedial action is selected.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make one command's separate invocation results visible for node A, node B and node C, including each target's status, output evidence, successful/failed/unresolved category and supplied scoped follow-up. Keep successful work and unresolved outcomes distinct from failures.

teaching_notes: Do not invent retry safety or remedial commands; use supplied target-specific follow-up.

required_facts.statement: Temporary credentials stop being usable after expiration and must be replaced with a newly authorized session.
On an expired-session error, renew the approved session through its credential provider and use the new access key, secret key and token together.
Before retrying a resource-changing operation, inspect its known outcome and use a supported idempotency token where the supplied operation offers one to avoid duplicate effects.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An approved session expired while an operational task was being handled. Renew the credentials, but first keep the known outcome of any resource-changing request in view before deciding to retry it.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Temporary credentials stop being usable after expiration and must be replaced with a newly authorized session.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
On an expired-session error, renew the approved session through its credential provider and use the new access key, secret key and token together.

Before retrying a resource-changing operation, inspect its known outcome and use a supported idempotency token where the supplied operation offers one to avoid duplicate effects.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
On the supplied expired-session error, renew through the approved credential provider and use the new access key, secret key and session token together. For a resource-changing request, inspect its known outcome before repeating it. Use a supported idempotency token where the supplied operation offers one. Record whether the original request is known to have taken effect instead of assuming an error always means no effect occurred.

Compare a known completed mutation with an operation whose result is unresolved. Renewed credentials are needed in either case, but the completed mutation should not be described as needing repetition simply because the caller later expired. For the unresolved case, inspect available outcome evidence before retrying and use the supplied operation's supported idempotency token where available. Valid identity and safe repeat behavior are separate questions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Renewing credentials does not settle a previous operation's outcome. Expired credentials must be replaced, but mutation retries require checking the known result and using supported idempotency where available to avoid duplicate effects.

video_need.reason: A short session-expiry and known-operation-outcome timeline helps explain safe renewal before mutation retry; text covers the rules.

practice_anchor.objective: Recover one supplied resource-changing automation operation from an expired session using the approved credential provider, without extending permissions. Inspect the operation's known outcome before deciding whether to retry, and use its supported idempotency token if a retry is warranted.
practice_anchor.success: The expired session is replaced through the approved provider with the new access key, secret key and session token used together, without displaying credential values or changing permissions. The learner checks the supplied outcome evidence, avoids repeating a known completed operation, and uses the supplied supported idempotency token for any warranted retry.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make session expiration and safe retry decisions visible as separate checks: replace the expired credential set through the approved provider, inspect the original operation's known outcome, avoid repeating a completed mutation, and use supported idempotency when retrying is warranted.

teaching_notes: Do not expose credentials or claim every AWS operation supports idempotency tokens.

required_facts.statement: The ECS task role supplies credentials for AWS calls made by the application containers.
The task execution role authorizes ECS startup work such as pulling an image and publishing logs; it is distinct from application AWS permissions.
Set taskRoleArn to the approved least-privilege application role in the task definition and test allowed and denied application operations from the task.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An ECS task starts, yet its application still needs AWS permissions. Separate the task execution role's startup work from the task role used by application containers.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The ECS task role supplies credentials for AWS calls made by the application containers.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
The task execution role authorizes ECS startup work such as pulling an image and publishing logs; it is distinct from application AWS permissions.

Set taskRoleArn to the approved least-privilege application role in the task definition and test allowed and denied application operations from the task.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: In the supplied task definition, set taskRoleArn to the approved least-privilege application role. From the task, test the supplied allowed and denied application operations. Inspect those results under the task's application identity. The execution role covers startup work such as image pulling and log publication; those capabilities do not substitute for the application role's permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: The task execution role is not the task role. Successful image pulling or log publication does not establish application AWS access. Set and test the approved taskRoleArn for application calls.

video_need.reason: A simple two-role task diagram helps distinguish startup operations from application calls; text supplies the complete bounded test.

practice_anchor.objective: Assign the approved least-privilege application role to taskRoleArn in a supplied ECS task definition, then run the supplied allowed and denied application operations from the task.
practice_anchor.success: taskRoleArn references the approved application role, the allowed application operation succeeds, and the denied application operation returns an access denial. The task execution role remains unchanged.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show two distinct permission paths: the task execution role authorizes ECS startup work, including image pulling and log publication; the task role referenced by taskRoleArn supplies credentials for application AWS calls. Associate the allowed and denied application test results with the task role.

teaching_notes: Do not broaden startup permissions to cover application work; use approved roles.

context.concept_name: Apply an approved security baseline to sandbox accounts

coverage.learning_objective: Apply an approved account security baseline

required_facts.statement: A governed account baseline applies standardized organizational controls and configuration to accounts.
Apply the supplied approved control configuration to the sandbox account and inspect each stated control’s deployment or evaluation result.
Distinguish preventive controls that restrict actions from detective controls that report noncompliance when interpreting the baseline checks.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A sandbox account needs the approved governed baseline. Apply the supplied control configuration, then check each control's actual deployment or evaluation result.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A governed account baseline applies standardized organizational controls and configuration to accounts.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Apply the supplied approved control configuration to the sandbox account and inspect each stated control’s deployment or evaluation result.

Distinguish preventive controls that restrict actions from detective controls that report noncompliance when interpreting the baseline checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use the approved sandbox control configuration and inspect every stated checkpoint. For a supplied preventive control, interpret its result as a restriction on actions. For a supplied detective control, interpret evaluation as reporting noncompliance. Record those different results by control rather than treating all baseline settings as equivalent barriers. The task applies an established baseline; it does not design new organizational security controls.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Preventive and detective controls do different work. A detective noncompliance report is not itself the preventive restriction, and the presence of baseline configuration is not the per-control verification result.

video_need.reason: A short baseline checkpoint walkthrough helps locate preventive deployment and detective evaluation evidence without designing new controls.

practice_anchor.objective: Apply one supplied approved baseline to the designated sandbox account, inspect every stated control's deployment or evaluation result, and record the control-check results.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied approved configuration is applied to the designated sandbox account. Every stated control has a recorded deployment or evaluation result, with preventive controls interpreted as action restrictions and detective controls interpreted as noncompliance reporting. No additional controls are introduced.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the designated sandbox account's applied baseline and per-control checkpoints, distinguishing preventive deployment results from detective evaluation results.

teaching_notes: Use supplied approved controls only; do not add organizational-policy behaviors absent from the brief.

context.concept_name: Apply bounded EKS workload configuration and secrets after external configuration/secrets preparation

coverage.learning_objective: Inject configuration into an EKS workload

required_facts.statement: A ConfigMap supplies nonconfidential configuration separately from the container image.
Reference a ConfigMap with envFrom.configMapRef or env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef in the supplied Pod template.
Reference a Secret with env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef or a secret-backed volume and test the consuming workload without printing the secret values.
Secrets require access control and appropriate storage protection; base64 encoding is not encryption.

misconceptions.statement: Environment variables populated from a ConfigMap do not automatically update inside already-running containers when the ConfigMap changes.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied EKS workload needs ordinary configuration and a secret without rebuilding its image or displaying the secret. Select the intended references and test the consumer's safe behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A ConfigMap supplies nonconfidential configuration separately from the container image.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Reference a ConfigMap with envFrom.configMapRef or env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef in the supplied Pod template.

Reference a Secret with env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef or a secret-backed volume and test the consuming workload without printing the secret values.

Secrets require access control and appropriate storage protection; base64 encoding is not encryption.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Reference the supplied ConfigMap through envFrom.configMapRef or env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef in the Pod template. Reference the supplied Secret through env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef or the prepared secret-backed volume. Test the consuming workload without printing secret values. A ConfigMap is for nonconfidential configuration; the Secret still needs access control and storage protection because base64 encoding is not encryption. If the exercise changes a ConfigMap used for environment variables, do not expect values in already-running containers to update automatically. Keep the consumer check tied to the actual supplied configuration and secret references.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Base64 encoding is not encryption. Also, ConfigMap-backed environment variables do not automatically update inside already-running containers after the ConfigMap changes. Test the intended consumer and protect secret values instead of exposing them for inspection.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content: Environment variables populated from a ConfigMap do not automatically update inside already-running containers when the ConfigMap changes.

video_need.reason: Pod-template references and consumer behavior, including unchanged running-container environment values, benefit from a configuration demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure the supplied Deployment's Pod template with references to the supplied ConfigMap and Secret, then use the supplied safe consumer check to verify consumption without displaying secret values.
practice_anchor.success: The Pod template references the intended ConfigMap and Secret names and keys, and the supplied consumer check confirms successful consumption without exposing secret values.

live_code.required_skill: Edit configuration and secret references within a supplied Deployment Pod template.
allowed_syntax: YAML mappings and lists within the supplied Deployment
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide the supplied Deployment with its existing container names and image unchanged, the supplied ConfigMap and Secret reference names and keys, and a prepared consumer check that reports success or failure without returning secret values.
live_code.observable_success: Only the intended Pod-template references are added. They match the supplied objects and keys, and the prepared check reports successful configuration and secret consumption without displaying secret values.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied Deployment's Pod-template references visible, connecting ConfigMap and Secret names and keys to their consuming environment variables while keeping secret values hidden.

teaching_notes: Use supplied configuration/secret objects; avoid secret display and untaught rollout/update procedures.

context.concept_name: Configure CodePipeline source-to-deploy actions; directly require native IAM identity-policy evaluation and role trust for the service execution role, not pipeline federation

required_facts.statement: A pipeline has stages containing actions that pass declared input and output artifacts between source, build and deployment operations.
Configure source output, CodeBuild input/output and CodeDeploy input artifact names so each action receives the intended revision’s output.
The CodePipeline service role requires trust for codepipeline.amazonaws.com and permissions for its actions and artifact access; this service role is not GitHub OIDC federation.
Verify action execution evidence carries the intended source revision through deployment and a failed action prevents normal progression to dependent actions.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A source revision must flow through CodePipeline build and deployment actions as the intended artifacts. Map declared input/output names first, then verify action evidence follows that revision.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A pipeline has stages containing actions that pass declared input and output artifacts between source, build and deployment operations.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure source output, CodeBuild input/output and CodeDeploy input artifact names so each action receives the intended revision’s output.

The CodePipeline service role requires trust for codepipeline.amazonaws.com and permissions for its actions and artifact access; this service role is not GitHub OIDC federation.

Verify action execution evidence carries the intended source revision through deployment and a failed action prevents normal progression to dependent actions.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the source output artifact name with the CodeBuild input, then its output with the CodeDeploy input. The supplied names must connect the intended revision's output between the actions. Inspect the CodePipeline service role's trust for codepipeline.amazonaws.com and its required action/artifact permissions. This is service-role authority, not GitHub OIDC federation. Run the supplied pipeline case and follow action evidence from the source revision through deployment. In the failure case, check that a failed action prevents normal progression to dependent actions. Keep the revision and artifact names with the execution evidence so that a successful action on a different input is not mistaken for the intended release.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A stage list alone does not establish artifact continuity. Actions pass declared artifacts, and their input/output names must connect correctly. Also, CodePipeline service-role trust is not interchangeable with GitHub OIDC trust.

video_need.reason: Revision-specific artifact links, action dependencies and CodePipeline service authority benefit from a pipeline-flow diagram.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure the supplied source, CodeBuild build and CodeDeploy EC2 deployment actions in a CodePipeline simulation. Connect their declared artifact names and select the supplied service execution role after checking its service trust and action/artifact permissions.
practice_anchor.success: Source output matches CodeBuild input, and CodeBuild output matches CodeDeploy input. The selected role trusts codepipeline.amazonaws.com and permits the supplied actions and artifact access. Execution evidence links the intended source revision to deployment; the supplied failed-action case shows no normal progression to dependent actions.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show stages containing source, CodeBuild and CodeDeploy actions, with declared output-to-input artifact links and the intended source revision traced through deployment. Include the CodePipeline service role's trust and permissions, plus a failed-action state that stops progression to dependent actions.

teaching_notes: Use supplied action structure and roles; do not introduce Jenkins/GitLab or independent application builds.

context.concept_name: Deploy a supplied CloudFormation S3 environment across accounts and Regions with assumed roles; directly require the native S3 object-storage concept

coverage.learning_objective: Deploy a supplied CloudFormation S3 environment across accounts and Regions

required_facts.statement: The same CloudFormation template can provision equivalent resource declarations in multiple approved target environments.

For each approved account/Region pair, use a named role profile with role_arn and source_profile, verify its caller with aws sts get-caller-identity --profile NAME, and create the supplied stack with that profile and explicit --region REGION.
Inspect stack outputs and S3 bucket identity and location in every intended target and check the supplied unapproved targets received no stack.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: The same approved S3 environment template must be deployed to several bounded account/Region targets. Verify each target's assumed caller and live stack identity rather than assuming the first successful deployment covers the rest.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The same CloudFormation template can provision equivalent resource declarations in multiple approved target environments.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
For each approved account/Region pair, use a named role profile with role_arn and source_profile, verify its caller with aws sts get-caller-identity --profile NAME, and create the supplied stack with that profile and explicit --region REGION.

Inspect stack outputs and S3 bucket identity and location in every intended target and check the supplied unapproved targets received no stack.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For each supplied approved account/Region pair, use its named role profile configured with role_arn and source_profile. Check get-caller-identity under that profile, then create the supplied stack with the profile and explicit Region. Inspect outputs, bucket identity and bucket location in every intended target. Check that the supplied unapproved targets received no stack. Keep a per-target record instead of one shared success label.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Equivalent declarations are not a single shared deployment result. Verify caller, stack outputs and bucket location in every approved target, and check the unapproved-target boundary separately.

video_need.reason: Repeated explicit-profile deployments benefit from a short per-target identity/output comparison; text fully specifies the bounded checks.

practice_anchor.objective: Deploy the same supplied CloudFormation S3 template to exactly two approved sandbox account/Region pairs. Use each target's named role profile configured with role_arn and source_profile, verify its caller with aws sts get-caller-identity --profile NAME, and create the stack with that profile and explicit --region REGION. Inspect each stack's outputs and bucket identity and location, then check the supplied unapproved targets for absence of the stack.
practice_anchor.success: A per-target record confirms that both approved targets have the expected caller account, successfully created stacks, and S3 bucket identities and locations matching their stack outputs and approved Regions. Checks of every supplied unapproved target confirm that no deployment stack is present; an access error does not count as proof of absence.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied account/Region matrix with approval status, named role profile, verified caller account, stack status, stack output bucket identity, observed bucket location, and unapproved-target absence results. Keep the two approved deployment results separate and distinguish confirmed absence from failed checks.

teaching_notes: Deploy the same supplied template; do not design new cross-account infrastructure or target discovery.

context.concept_name: Diagnose AWS connectivity failures using prepared DNS, HTTP, ports and CIDR foundations

required_facts.statement: The subnet’s route table must contain a matching destination route to a usable target for the required network path.
Check DNS resolution and the intended endpoint address using the supplied tools, then inspect route association, required protocol/port rules and response traffic to localize the failing layer.
Network ACLs are stateless, so required requests and responses need permitted traffic in their respective directions.
Make the approved correction supported by the failing layer’s evidence and repeat the endpoint connection test.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An endpoint connection fails, but the symptom does not identify the failing layer. Use the supplied tools and path evidence to localize the issue before making an approved correction.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The subnet’s route table must contain a matching destination route to a usable target for the required network path.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Check DNS resolution and the intended endpoint address using the supplied tools, then inspect route association, required protocol/port rules and response traffic to localize the failing layer.

Network ACLs are stateless, so required requests and responses need permitted traffic in their respective directions.

Make the approved correction supported by the failing layer’s evidence and repeat the endpoint connection test.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Check DNS resolution and the intended endpoint address first with the supplied tools. Inspect the subnet's route-table association and destination route to a usable target, then the required protocol/port rules and response traffic. For a supplied network-ACL case, evaluate requests and responses in their respective directions because ACLs are stateless. If the evidence localizes the failure to a missing response allowance, use the approved correction for that layer rather than altering every control in the path. Repeat the endpoint connection test after correction. This example applies completed external DNS, HTTP/HTTPS and ports/firewall preparation; it does not recreate those foundations or infer a route problem from every connection error.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A permitted request direction is not enough for a stateless network ACL. Required responses need permitted traffic in their direction too. Also, an edited route table is not evidence of the used association; inspect the actual path and retest.

video_need.reason: DNS, actual route association and bidirectional controls form a connection path whose localized failure benefits from layered visual diagnosis.

media.group_title: Why permitted requests can still fail at a network ACL

segments.label: How a network ACL can block a permitted request's response
segments.summary: Security groups automatically permit response traffic for an allowed request. Network ACLs are stateless: inbound and outbound traffic are evaluated separately. In the example, assuming an inbound rule permits the request, an outbound deny rule prevents the response from reaching the caller. Network ACL deny rules can apply to individual IP addresses or CIDR ranges. A permitted request therefore does not establish that its response can pass.

bridge_note.before: Watch how an outbound deny blocks a response. This example assumes inbound traffic is explicitly allowed; the speaker's wording about no matching inbound rule does not mean unmatched traffic is allowed.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains stateless response filtering, not the full diagnosis. The text covers DNS and endpoint checks, actual route association, matching routes to usable targets, protocol/port checks, approved correction and endpoint retesting.

practice_anchor.objective: Resolve one seeded endpoint failure in a supplied sandbox topology using supplied DNS and connection tools, route-association evidence, and protocol/port and network-ACL rules. Apply only the approved correction supported by the failing layer's evidence.
practice_anchor.success: The learner identifies the broken layer from the supplied evidence, applies the approved correction without changing unrelated controls, and repeats the endpoint connection test to confirm that the connection succeeds.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied endpoint path visible, including DNS resolution to the intended address, the subnet's actual route-table association and matching route target, and request and response directions through network controls. Mark the evidence-supported failing layer and show the successful connection after correction.

teaching_notes: Require external networking preparation; do not add command syntax or control behaviors absent from allowed facts.

context.concept_name: Execute an established fleet patch task after external package-management and shell preparation

coverage.learning_objective: Execute an established fleet patch task

required_facts.statement: Patch Manager uses patch baselines and managed-node targets to scan or install patches and report compliance.
Use the established maintenance-window task with the approved target set, patch document parameters, concurrency and error limits.
Inspect task execution and per-node patch compliance results to verify which approved instances were patched and which require follow-up.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An established patch task should operate on only the approved managed nodes. Preserve the maintenance-window bounds and inspect per-node compliance afterwards.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Patch Manager uses patch baselines and managed-node targets to scan or install patches and report compliance.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the established maintenance-window task with the approved target set, patch document parameters, concurrency and error limits.

Inspect task execution and per-node patch compliance results to verify which approved instances were patched and which require follow-up.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Use the supplied maintenance-window task, approved targets, patch-document parameters, concurrency and error limits. Inspect execution results and each node's patch compliance result. If one node needs follow-up while others are patched, record that distinction with the target IDs. Patch Manager scans or installs using baselines and reports compliance; the scheduled task alone is not evidence that every approved node was patched.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Task execution is not the full per-node compliance check. Verify which approved instances were patched and which require follow-up, retaining the supplied concurrency and error limits rather than widening the task.

video_need.reason: A short maintenance-window execution and per-node compliance inspection helps locate evidence while text supplies the scope limits.

media.group_title: Patch baselines, managed-node targets, and compliance

segments.label: How baseline rules and managed-node targets govern scan and install results
segments.summary: Patch Manager uses patch baselines to define which available patches are applicable and approved. Operations can run immediately or on a schedule against Systems Manager managed nodes, including targets selected by key/value pairs. A scan checks applicable patches against the baseline and reports noncompliance when required patches are missing. An install applies patches with the aim of bringing the node into compliance with that baseline. AWS provides predefined baselines as examples, not recommended best practices; for this task, retain the already-approved configuration.

bridge_note.before: Watch how baseline rules and managed-node targets lead to scan or install results. The clip calls predefined baselines recommendations; treat them as examples, and retain your already-approved configuration.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains the patching model, not established maintenance-window execution or per-node result inspection. The text covers approved targets, document parameters, concurrency and error limits, and verification of patched nodes and follow-up needs.

practice_anchor.objective: Run one supplied maintenance-window patch task on a small sandbox fleet, retaining its approved targets, patch-document parameters, concurrency and error limits.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied task runs with its approved configuration unchanged. Execution recipients are compared with the approved target IDs, and execution evidence and per-node patch compliance results are used to record which instances were patched and which require follow-up.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied maintenance-window task's approved targets, patch-document parameters, concurrency and error limits visible alongside task execution recipients and per-node patch compliance results, so each approved target ID can be linked to its outcome and follow-up needs.

teaching_notes: Require external Linux package-management and fleet preparation; use established patch tasks only.

context.concept_name: Expose an EKS workload using a Kubernetes Service

coverage.learning_objective: Expose an EKS workload through a Service

required_facts.statement: A Kubernetes Service provides a stable network endpoint for a changing set of selected Pods.
Set spec.selector to match the intended Pod labels and ports.port and ports.targetPort to map the Service port to the application’s container port.
Apply the supplied Service, inspect its EndpointSlices or endpoints and test the Service address from the supplied client to verify selected Pods receive traffic.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A Kubernetes Service should reach the supplied application even as selected Pods change. Connect its selector and port mapping with actual selected endpoints, then test from the supplied client.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Kubernetes Service provides a stable network endpoint for a changing set of selected Pods.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set spec.selector to match the intended Pod labels and ports.port and ports.targetPort to map the Service port to the application’s container port.

Apply the supplied Service, inspect its EndpointSlices or endpoints and test the Service address from the supplied client to verify selected Pods receive traffic.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Set spec.selector to match the intended Pod labels and map ports.port to the application's ports.targetPort. Apply the supplied Service and inspect its EndpointSlices or endpoints. Test the Service address from the supplied client to verify traffic reaches the selected Pods. Keep selector, endpoint and client-result evidence together rather than accepting a Service object name as proof of application reachability.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A Service declaration is not the traffic test. Its selector must match the intended Pods, its targetPort must map to the application port, and observed endpoints/client results verify the intended path.

video_need.reason: A Service selector, selected endpoints and port mapping benefit from a request-path diagram and supplied client result.

practice_anchor.objective: Create one Service for the supplied Deployment using the supplied access and apply procedure. Match its selector to the intended Pod labels, map the Service port to the application's container port, inspect EndpointSlices or endpoints, and test the Service address from the supplied client.
practice_anchor.success: The applied Service selects the intended Pods and maps its port to the application's container port. EndpointSlice or endpoint evidence identifies those Pods, and the supplied client receives the expected application response through the Service address.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the request path visible from the supplied client through the stable Service address and Service port to selected Pod endpoints and the application's container port. Annotate the selector-to-label match and associate the path with endpoint evidence and the client result.

teaching_notes: Use supplied apply/access procedure; do not introduce cluster networking administration or unsupported Service types.

clusters.title: Before-and-after fleet execution checks
clusters.reasoning: Both concepts apply to a scoped fleet operation: inspect proposed targets and actions before mutation, then classify target-specific outcomes before selecting follow-up. Their shared remote-command prerequisite is earlier than the tile, and required external fleet/shell preparation must already be complete. Preserve the distinction between limited dry-run permission evidence and actual invocation results; neither concept must be learned to satisfy the other's entry prerequisites.
